title: Best Embedded Integration Platforms for SaaS Compared
summary: Best embedded integration platform for SaaS varies by use case.
body_markdown:
## 2. Pipedream for customer authentication and APIs


Pipedream Connect lets your product handle customer authentication and call APIs across a very large app catalogue, while your own engineers write the integration logic in code. Commercially, you trade a visual builder your customers can use for control over exactly what each integration does.


The catalogue is the draw.


Pipedream's stated app count rose from 700+ in 2022 to 1,000+ in 2023 and 2,100+ in 2024, and now stands at 3,000+, so a customer request for an app is increasingly one where you don't have to build and maintain the OAuth handshake yourself.


On the page, the chart sits here.


What follows from that is a division of labour. Pipedream manages the credentials: your customer connects their account inside your product, and Pipedream stores and refreshes the tokens.


Your code then calls the app's API with those credentials, either directly or through Pipedream's workflows, which are written in code and can be triggered from your backend.


For a team that already writes integration logic, that's a short path from "we need a Slack or CRM connection" to a shipped feature.


### Pipedream Connect limitations for workflows


Seen from the other side, the main limit is the same property. Connect gives your customers a way to authorise apps, not a workflow editor they can reshape.


If your customers need to design their own automations, you would be building that interface yourself on top of it. Count that engineering time against the catalogue savings.


Activepieces ships that interface already, and a missing connector doesn't wait on a vendor release: if the app a customer asks for isn't among its 750 integrations, you can have AI build the missing one and keep it private to your own instance.


The 750 is the number of integrations in the` packages/pieces/community` directory of the MIT-licensed open-source repository on GitHub, so you can count it yourself rather than take a marketing figure on trust, and roughly 60% of what's in that directory was contributed by the community, so the platform's future depends on volunteers staying engaged.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it in production.


You will find pricing and usage limits on Pipedream's own pricing page, and they change. I haven't quoted figures here because I couldn't confirm them for this article.


Read that page on the day you decide, with your expected number of connected customer accounts and monthly workflow runs in hand. Those are the two volumes a product-embedded setup scales on.


Pipedream Connect suits a SaaS company with developers available that wants a fixed set of integrations it controls end to end, across many apps, without owning authentication for each one. It suits you less if the plan is for customers to build their own workflows.
